source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Skin turgor is unrelated to hydration assessment and should never be examined clinically","B":"Skin turgor is more reliable in older adults because aging increases dermal elasticity","C":"Skin turgor alone is sufficient to rule out dehydration when recoil appears normal","D":"Skin turgor is less reliable in older adults because normal aging reduces skin elasticity"}}
source_row.rationale: Age-related loss of skin elasticity makes skin turgor less reliable for assessing dehydration in older adults. Hydration assessment should incorporate additional findings rather than relying on turgor alone.
source_row.source_detail: Review of hydration assessment in adults ≥65 years: reduced skin turgor and multiple other classic clinical signs lack sufficient diagnostic accuracy; skin turgor correlates with age more than hydration status.
source_row.source_name: Deißler et al. — Hydration Status Assessment in Older Patients (2023)
source_row.stem: An older adult has poor oral intake and possible dehydration. How should the nurse interpret skin turgor during the assessment?
